title: Increasing a topic's partition count from 6 to 12 — what silently breaks (key-to-partition mapping)?
shortTitle: Increasing a topic's partition count from 6 to 12 — what silently breaks (key-to-partition mapping)?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka's default partitioner places a keyed record using the formula `partition = murmur2(key) mod numPartitions`. The chosen partition therefore depends on the total number of partitions. When you increase a topic from six to twelve partitions, the modulo divisor changes, so the same key can now map to a completely different partition. What silently breaks is per-key ordering: records for a given key that were previously all funneled into one partition are now split across old and new partitions, and Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition, not across partitions.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sorts customer letters into pigeonholes by taking the account number, running it through a fixed rule, and using the remainder when dividing by the number of pigeonholes. With six pigeonholes, all of Rajesh's letters always land in pigeonhole 3, so they are read strictly in the order they arrived. Now the mailroom adds six more pigeonholes to total twelve and keeps using the same rule. Overnight the remainder for Rajesh's account changes, so his new letters start landing in pigeonhole 9 while his old unread letters are still sitting in pigeonhole 3. Two different clerks now read Rajesh's letters, and nobody guarantees which clerk reads first. His debit might be processed before the deposit that was supposed to come first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Adding partitions changes the modulo divisor in `hash(key) mod numPartitions`, so existing keys get remapped and per-key ordering silently breaks across the split between old and new partitions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka's default partitioner places a keyed record using the formula `partition = murmur2(key) mod numPartitions`. The chosen partition therefore depends on the total number of partitions. When you increase a topic from six to twelve partitions, the modulo divisor changes, so the same key can now map to a completely different partition. What silently breaks is per-key ordering: records for a given key that were previously all funneled into one partition are now split across old and new partitions, and Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition, not across partitions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sorts customer letters into pigeonholes by taking the account number, running it through a fixed rule, and using the remainder when dividing by the number of pigeonholes. With six pigeonholes, all of Rajesh's letters always land in pigeonhole 3, so they are read strictly in the order they arrived. Now the mailroom adds six more pigeonholes to total twelve and keeps using the same rule. Overnight the remainder for Rajesh's account changes, so his new letters start landing in pigeonhole 9 while his old unread letters are still sitting in pigeonhole 3. Two different clerks now read Rajesh's letters, and nobody guarantees which clerk reads first. His debit might be processed before the deposit that was supposed to come first.

**One line to remember:** Adding partitions changes the modulo divisor in `hash(key) mod numPartitions`, so existing keys get remapped and per-key ordering silently breaks across the split between old and new partitions.

sections.s2_technical:
The heart of the issue is the default partitioner. For a record with a non-null key, Kafka computes a 32-bit murmur2 hash of the serialized key bytes and then takes that hash modulo the number of partitions. In pseudocode the producer does `partition = Utils.toPositive(Utils.murmur2(keyBytes)) % numPartitions;`. Because `numPartitions` is part of the formula, changing it changes the output for most keys. For example, if `murmur2("SAV2001")` produces a value whose remainder modulo six is three, the remainder of that same value modulo twelve is very unlikely to also be three.

The first thing that breaks is ordering per key. Kafka's only ordering guarantee is within a single partition: records in one partition are delivered in offset order, but there is no ordering guarantee across partitions. Before the change, every event for account SAV2001 went to one partition and was processed in order. After the increase, old events for SAV2001 might still be unread in the original partition while new events land in a new partition. A consumer group with one consumer per partition will read these two partitions independently and concurrently, so the new events can be processed before the leftover old events. In a banking ledger, that means a reversal could be applied before the original transaction, or a balance update could be applied out of sequence.

The second thing to understand is that this is silent. Kafka does not throw an error, log a warning, or reject the operation. The command `kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions 12` succeeds instantly and everything looks healthy. Throughput might even improve. The only symptom is subtle data correctness bugs that appear later, which makes this one of the most dangerous "harmless looking" operations in Kafka.

A third important point is that you can never decrease partitions to undo this. Kafka does not support reducing partition count because that would require merging data and would corrupt key placement even further, so the only way back is to create a new topic and migrate. There is also a related breakage for stateful stream processing: Kafka Streams and other frameworks store per-key state keyed by partition, and repartitioning invalidates the co-location assumption between a key and its state store, which can require a full application reset.

The senior-level fixes are the following. The cleanest option is to size partitions correctly up front so you rarely need to add them. If you must scale and ordering matters, create a brand-new topic with the target partition count and a custom or default partitioner, then migrate producers and consumers to it, optionally draining the old topic first so no key has in-flight records split across both topics. If you cannot change topics, you can pin key placement with a custom partitioner that maps a key to a stable partition independent of the raw modulo, for example by hashing into a fixed number of logical buckets, but you must deploy that partitioner before the repartition and understand it still cannot fix records already written under the old scheme. The one case where adding partitions is safe is when records have null keys, because they are distributed round-robin and carry no per-key ordering expectation in the first place.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India publishes every ledger event for an account to the `account.ledger` topic, keyed by account id, so that all events for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) stay in order within their own partition. A downstream service rebuilds each account's running balance by replaying these events in order.

Problem 1 — during a traffic surge, an engineer increased `account.ledger` from six to twelve partitions to get more parallelism. The command succeeded instantly with no warning. This is exactly the modulo-divisor problem: the partitioner formula changed from mod six to mod twelve, so the destination partition for most account ids changed.

Problem 2 — a few minutes later, the balance service reported a wrong balance for Rajesh. His latest events were landing in a new partition and being applied before two older events that were still queued in his original partition. This is exactly the per-key ordering breakage: ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, and his key now straddled two partitions.

Our runnable demo makes this visible. It computes the destination partition for the same set of account ids under six partitions and under twelve partitions using the real murmur2-style formula, counts how many keys get remapped, and then simulates replaying two events for a remapped key to show how a debit can be applied before the deposit once the key is split. The classes are `PartitionRemapDemo` (driver), `DefaultPartitioner` (the hash-mod formula), `StickyBucketPartitioner` (the safe fix using fixed logical buckets), and `LedgerReplay` (shows the ordering break).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the Spring producer service
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -jar target/ledger-publisher-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# Safe way to scale: create a NEW topic at the target size, migrate, then retire the old one
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic account.ledger.v2 --partitions 12 \
  --replication-factor 3 --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092

# Run the demo to see how many keys get remapped on 6 -> 12
javac demo/PartitionRemapDemo.java -d out
java -cp out com.bank.ledger.demo.PartitionRemapDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: eight account ids published to `account.ledger`, first with six partitions, then after an increase to twelve partitions.

Step 1: With six partitions, each account id is hashed with murmur2 and the hash is taken modulo six. Every event for SAV2001 lands in the same partition, say partition 3, so all of Rajesh's events are strictly ordered.

Step 2: An operator runs the alter command to move the topic to twelve partitions. The command returns instantly and no error is logged. Nothing appears wrong.

Step 3: The producer now computes the hash modulo twelve. For most account ids the remainder changes. In the demo, several of the eight keys map to a different partition under twelve than under six. SAV2001 now resolves to a new partition such as partition 9.

Step 4: At the moment of the change, SAV2001 still has an older CREDIT event with sequence 1 sitting unread in partition 3. A newer DEBIT event with sequence 2 is produced and goes to partition 9. Two different consumer threads own those two partitions and read them independently.

Step 5: The consumer thread on partition 9 reads sequence 2 and applies the debit before the consumer thread on partition 3 reads sequence 1. The balance service applies events out of order and computes a wrong balance for Rajesh. The guard is a per-account expected sequence check that rejects any event whose sequence is not exactly last applied plus one, which at least turns a silent corruption into a detectable error.

Final output:

    │
    ├─ BEFORE (6 partitions)                       ├─ AFTER (alter to 12 partitions)

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Partitioner Design and Ordering Guard ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy Pattern: Partitioner (Default vs StickyBucket)          │
  │     WHY: swap placement policy without changing producer code     │
  │  Guard Clause: per-account expected-sequence check on consumer    │
  │     WHY: fail loud on out-of-order instead of corrupting balance  │

  │  S: Partitioner only places records; BalanceService only applies │
  │  O: new placement policy = new Partitioner implementation         │
  │  D: producer depends on Partitioner interface, not a concrete one │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> Partitioner  │
  │ + partition(topic,key,...)   │
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
        ┌──────────┴───────────┐
        ▼                      ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ DefaultPartitioner│  │ StickyBucketPartitioner  │
  │ murmur2(key) %    │  │ - buckets: int (fixed=24)│
  │   numPartitions   │  │ bucket = murmur2(key)%24 │
  │ (breaks on resize)│  │ return bucket % numParts │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Ledger Event Apply ──────────────────────────────

  [RECEIVED] ──seq == last+1?── yes ──→ [APPLIED] (balance updated, last_seq++)
        │                                   
        └── no (gap or dup) ──→ [REJECTED/HELD] ──→ alert, wait for missing seq

  ── Call Chain (safe scaling) ──────────────────────────────────────

  1. create account.ledger.v2 (12 partitions)
  2. producer.send(record, StickyBucketPartitioner)   // stable bucket->partition
  3.   bucket = murmur2(accountId) % 24
  4.   partition = bucket % currentPartitionCount
  5. consumer.poll() -> for each event: assert seq == last_seq_no + 1
  6.   if ok: apply + persist; else: reject + alert
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka decides where a keyed record goes using the formula hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, with the hash computed by murmur2. The number of partitions is part of that formula, so if you increase a topic from six partitions to twelve, the divisor changes and most existing keys now resolve to a different partition. The command to add partitions succeeds instantly with no warning, which is why people call this change harmless, but what silently breaks is per-key ordering, because Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition and never across partitions.

The concrete danger is that a key which used to live entirely in one partition is now split: its newer records land in a new partition while its older records may still be unread in the original partition, and because those two partitions are consumed independently, the newer records can be processed before the older ones. In a banking context on the National Bank of India ledger, that is exactly how you end up applying a debit before the deposit it depended on, or a reversal before the original transaction, and the resulting balance is wrong even though nothing errored.

The reason this is so dangerous is that it is completely silent, it can even look like a performance win because you got more parallelism, and you cannot simply undo it, because Kafka does not allow reducing the partition count. So the fix is mostly about doing it right the first time. I size partitions generously up front so I rarely need to add them. When I genuinely must scale and ordering matters, I create a brand-new topic at the target partition count, migrate producers and consumers to it, and drain or dual-produce so that no single key has records straddling both topics during the switch. Where I control the producer, I also use a custom partitioner that hashes keys into a fixed number of logical buckets and then maps buckets onto the current partitions, which keeps placement stable even if the partition count changes later.

Finally, I always add a defensive guard on the consumer: a per-account expected sequence number, so that if ordering ever does break, the system rejects the out-of-order event and raises an alert instead of silently corrupting a balance. That turns the scariest property of this change, its silence, into something observable. The one safe exception I mention is topics with null keys, where records are spread round-robin and there is no per-key ordering expectation, so adding partitions there is genuinely harmless.
